title: Nuremberg Style Solar Clock
intro: This modern location-aware reconstruction adopts the Nuremberg-style day/night counting scheme but derives the daily allocation from local solar geometry instead of the city's fixed historical turning days.
structure: Round the computed daylight length to the nearest whole hour and restrict the day allocation to 8–16 hours. The rest belongs to night. Both intervals use equal ordinary hours. NUR-LD counts from day start; NUR-LN counts from night start. Scheduled boundaries are centred on apparent noon, not necessarily the exact sunrise and sunset.
example: A calculated daylight length of 13 hours 40 minutes gives a 14-hour day allocation. Day starts at 05:00 and ends at 19:00 apparent solar time. At apparent noon the display is 07:00 NUR-LD; at midnight it is 05:00 NUR-LN.
history: This profile adapts the historical principle of separate day and night counts to the selected location. It deliberately does not reproduce the 1488 civic Wendetag schedule.
model: Compute daylight from solar declination, latitude and a 0.833-degree horizon correction. Round floor(daylight hours + 0.5), clamp to 8–16, and set boundaries to (24-N)/2 and (24+N)/2. Compute local apparent solar time with east-positive longitude and equation of time. Floor elapsed hours, minutes and optional seconds, and search for the next changed display.
limits: Requires valid coordinates. Missing solar crossings produce N/A; invalid location fails. This is a compact modern solar approximation, not a historical Nuremberg clock record. Time zones and daylight saving do not determine the boundaries. The solar model assumes an idealised sea-level horizon and standard depression; local terrain and weather are not modelled.
